Here are some of the important healthcare stories from this week:
Novo Nordisk rebrands as ‘Novo’ in push to win back obesity market
Novo Nordisk
will
to Novo as the Danish drugmaker seeks to strengthen its brand as it battles Eli Lilly
for dominance in the obesity-drug market.

The company will also update its logo, with its trademark bull shifting to face right, Novo said Monday. The changes come as Lilly increasingly adopts a single-name identity, dropping “Eli” from its marketing materials.
At its Capital Markets Day on September 21 in London, Novo will provide a detailed overview of the updated corporate strategy.
CEO Mike Doustdar is pushing to make Novo leaner and more competitive as the company works to regain market share in obesity treatments.
Summit’s ivonescimab cuts death risk by 27% versus Keytruda in lung cancer trial
Summit Therapeutics
on Sunday said ivonescimab
compared with Merck’s
Keytruda in a late-stage lung cancer trial conducted by its partner Akeso
in China.

Ivonescimab reduced the risk of death by 27% compared with Keytruda, also known as pembrolizumab, among previously untreated patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer whose tumors expressed PD-L1.
Median overall survival reached 30.8 months for patients receiving ivonescimab, compared with 22.6 months for the Keytruda group. The 8.2-month difference was statistically significant, Summit said.

The Phase 3 HARMONi-2 trial enrolled 398 patients and had a median follow-up period of 36 months. Results are being presented at the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer’s World Conference on Lung Cancer in Seoul.
GE HealthCare is said to near $1B Sofie Biosciences deal
GE HealthCare Technologies

is in advanced talks to acquire Sofie Biosciences for about $1 billion, a move that would expand its presence in radioactive diagnostic agents used with medical scans, the Financial Times reported Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter.
The companies could announce a transaction as soon as next week, although negotiations may still change or fall apart. GE HealthCare
, Sofie and private equity investor Trilantic declined or did not respond to requests for comment.

Sofie develops radiopharmaceuticals and operates a network that produces the short-lived radioactive materials used in positron emission tomography, or PET, scans. Its pipeline includes diagnostic agents designed to detect certain gastroesophageal and pancreatic cancers.
Buying Sofie would strengthen GE HealthCare’s

pharmaceutical diagnostics business, which supplies substances administered to patients before imaging procedures. It also would give the company a larger position in a fast-growing field that combines specialized drugs with the scanners GE HealthCare
already sells.
Lilly wins full FDA approval for Inluriyo combo in breast cancer
Eli Lilly

on Friday announced that the U.S. FDA granted full approval for an all-oral regimen containing its estrogen receptor antagonist Inluriyo and kinase inhibitor Verzenio as a late-line option for breast cancer.

Specifically, the approval clears the combo for adults with estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HER2-) breast cancer with an ESR1 mutation whose disease has progressed following one or more lines of prior endocrine therapy. The treatment is indicated for those with locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer.

The decision is based on data from the company’s Phase 3 EMBER-3 trial in which patients with ESR1-mutated MBC receiving Inluriyo with Verzenio as a late-line therapy doubled median progression-free survival compared to those who received Inluriyo alone.
Inluriyo belongs to a novel drug class known as oral selective estrogen receptor degraders. Roche’s
oral SERD giredestrant is currently under FDA priority review for ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, with a decision expected by Nov. 30.
Medtronic launches exchange offer to complete separation of MiniMed
Medtronic
has launched an exchange offer to split off at least 80.1% of MiniMed Group
, its former diabetes business.

The exchange offer will allow Medtronic shareholders to exchange their ordinary shares for MiniMed common stock at a 7% discount, subject to a maximum of 4.5939 MiniMed shares per Medtronic share tendered and accepted.
If the upper limit does not apply, shareholders are expected to receive approximately $107.53 worth of MiniMed stock for every $100 of Medtronic ordinary shares tendered.

MiniMed completed its IPO in March 2026, with Medtronic retaining about a 90% stake. Medtronic currently owns 252.8M shares of MiniMed common stock, representing ~90% of the total outstanding shares of MiniMed common stock.
